### Real case: primary HbA1c result at Week 28

**Question 2.6 — Was an appropriate analysis used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention?**  
**Permitted response: probably_no.**

The trial randomized participants individually to dulaglutide or placebo and included all 291 randomized participants in its stated intention-to-treat population (main article, p. 2, lines 91–104; p. 4, lines 1–3). But for efficacy, data were censored from rescue therapy or premature study-drug discontinuation; the figure caption confirms that the analyses excluded data after rescue or discontinuation (p. 3, lines 89–100; p. 5, lines 1–7). Thus the reported analysis did not retain all post-randomization outcome information under assignment. This could be an inappropriate post-randomization exclusion for the assignment effect.

The extent and exact mechanism remain unclear. The article says one participant received rescue therapy, in the dulaglutide group (p. 7, lines 7–9), but does not report how many participants had study-drug discontinuation before Week 28 with otherwise observed HbA1c values omitted from this analysis. Completion counts are not HbA1c measurement counts (main article, p. 4, lines 1–3; Figure 1 transcription, p. 4, lines 1–5). Registry results report 133 and 142 participants with baseline and at least one post-baseline HbA1c measurement, but do not establish who had Week 28 measurements or whether measured values after discontinuation were omitted (registry, p. 1, lines 1898–1920). The 139/147 counts and last-observation-carried-forward rule apply to supplementary composite outcomes, not the primary continuous HbA1c result (supplement, p. 1, lines 16–31; p. 2, lines 1–47).

The ITT label and balanced baseline summaries support assignment-based intent, but do not resolve the stated censoring rule. An alternative explanation is that few participants were actually affected: rescue was used by only one participant, and the report does not quantify primary-result exclusions attributable to discontinuation.

**Question 2.7 — If 2.6 is N/PN/NI, could the failure to analyze participants in their randomized group substantially affect this Result?**  
**Permitted response: probably_no.**

Only one rescue-therapy case is documented, and the discontinuation totals are modest relative to 291 randomized participants (main article, p. 7, lines 7–9; Figure 1 transcription, p. 4, lines 2–5). These facts make a substantial impact from the known rescue exclusion less likely. However, the primary analysis’s affected participant count and their HbA1c values or prognostic characteristics are not reported. Discontinuation may have selected participants whose outcomes differed, so a substantial effect cannot be ruled out confidently.

### Fictional controls: Question 2.6 only

**Control A — Permitted response: yes.**  
All 90 measured Week 12 outcomes are analyzed in assigned groups; the 10 exclusions are solely due to unmeasured endpoints and are independent of adherence. Outcomes are retained regardless of treatment stopping. This is an appropriate modified ITT analysis under the supplied guidance. No material mechanism uncertainty is stated in these complete facts.

**Control B — Permitted response: no.**  
All 100 endpoint values were measured, but the analysis omits the 10 noncompleters’ observed values based on treatment completion, despite retaining assigned groups. This is an adherence-conditioned post-randomization exclusion, not exclusion for missing outcome data, and no causal adjustment addresses it. The facts leave no material unknown about the exclusion mechanism.
